query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Enriching the HEA bond coat with additional aluminum promotes the in‐situ formation of a continuous, dense alumina (Al2O3) layer during HVOF processing, which increases coating durability and reliability under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy bond coat (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi or related compositions) deposited without extra aluminum enrichment, known to form non-uniform, less protective oxide scales under HVOF conditions.
generation.intervention: Incorporate additional aluminum into the HEA feedstock prior to HVOF deposition to increase the Al content in the coating.
generation.conditions: The treatment is applied during standard HVOF processing and performance is evaluated under high-temperature (e.g., ~1000°C) oxidation in air, simulating operational TBC environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The additional aluminum diffuses to the coating surface during the rapid thermal process, leading to the nucleation and growth of a continuous, protective Al2O3 layer.
generation.mechanism: Extra Al in the HEA promotes surface diffusion and reaction with available oxygen during HVOF deposition, forming a dense alumina scale that acts as a barrier to further oxidation and prevents the formation of less protective mixed oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-enriched bond coats will show a more uniform and adherent alumina scale, reduced oxide penetration and scale growth rate, and improved adhesion and durability compared to standard HEA coatings.
generation.baseline: Standard HEA bond coats (without extra aluminum) tend to form heterogeneous oxide scales—rich in Mn and mixed phases—that lead to inferior oxidation resistance and durability under prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected as long as the aluminum level remains within an optimal range that enhances alumina formation without significantly altering the desired phase equilibria or mechanical properties of the HEA. Extreme Al additions may destabilize the alloy or change its microstructural performance.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal aluminum enrichment level and the quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance and mechanical adhesion are not yet fully determined; further optimization and testing are needed to confirm the magnitude of benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA bond coat samples using HVOF deposition: one set with the standard composition and one set with a controlled, additional percentage of aluminum. Subject both groups to high-temperature oxidation testing (e.g., annealing in air at 1000°C for 50 hours). Evaluate the coatings using surface and cross-sectional SEM/EDS analysis, XRD to assess oxide phase formation, and adhesion testing.
measurements: Phase composition of oxide scales (XRD, EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-enriched samples do not form a significantly more continuous and protective Al2O3 scale—with measurable reductions in oxide growth rate and improved adhesion—compared to the standard HEA samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.

Oxidation and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder produced via gas atomization were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. The following was found:Under HVOF spraying, the processes of oxidation and phase transformations occur in the following sequence: (i) pronounced Al diffusion from subsurface BCC supersaturated solid solution to the particle surface; (ii) particle’s surface Al2O3 formation; and (iii) FCC formation in the Al-depleted subsurface layer.During continuous heating in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) Al diffusion to the surface; and (iii) simultaneous formation of Al2O3 and FCC due to Al outflow from BCC/B2.During prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) diffusion of Al, Cr, Fe, and Mo to the surface; and (iii) formation of surface Al2O3 and undersurface sigma due to enrichment of the undersurface zone with Cr

reading.lever: Enrich the HEA bond coat with additional aluminum to promote in-situ formation of a continuous, protective Al2O3 layer during HVOF processing.
reading.why: Prior HVOF studies on Al-containing HEAs demonstrated improved oxidation resistance via protective alumina formation, addressing durability issues in high-temperature TBC environments.
